summary: שַׁעַר is the gate: the opening in a city wall with its doors and bar, and the gate of a camp, of the tabernacle court, of Yahweh's house and of the king. The open place at the gate was where the elders sat, cases were judged and bargains witnessed (Rut 4:1, 11; Deu 21:19; Amo 5:15), so “your gates” are your towns, and the gate can stand for the city and its power: Abraham's seed “will possess the gate of his enemies” (Gen 22:17). The שֹׁעֵר is the one who keeps the gate, at a city and among the Levites at the house of Yahweh. Ugaritic ṯġr “gate, gatekeeper”, Arabic ṯaġr “gap, breach, frontier pass” and Aramaic תְּרַע (Daniel, Ezra, the Peshitta) show the older sounds ṯ and ġ behind ש and ע. A second older root, šʿr “reckon” (Arabic siʿr “price”), gives the verb of Pro 23:7 and the “hundred measures” of Gen 26:12; the words for a horrible thing (Jer 5:30; Hos 6:10) have no tie yet understood.

words.gloss: gate; the gate as the place of judgment; (pl.) towns
words.summary: About 370 times. The opening in a wall, with its doors, posts and bar, and the open place inside it where the city met. Its key in the database also takes Gen 26:12 (שְׁעָרִים “measures”) and Pro 23:7 (the verb), filed with it by spelling.

senses.gloss: gate (of a city, camp or court)
senses.definition: The opening in a city's wall, closed by doors with posts and a bar, by which men go in and out; also the entrance of the camp in the wilderness and of the tabernacle court.

evidence.note: Samson took hold of “the doors of the gate of the city (דַלְתוֹת שַׁעַר־ הָעִיר) and the two posts”, and pulled them up with the bar.
“All who went out of the gate of his city”: the men of the city are those who go in and out by its gate.
The manslayer stands “at the entrance of the gate of the city” and speaks to the elders.
David sits between the two gates; the watchman goes up to the roof of the gate, on the wall.
The wall of Jerusalem is broken down “and its gates burned with fire”.
“He has strengthened the bars of your gates.”
The gates of Jerusalem are shut before the sabbath and men set at the gates, so that no load comes in.
Doors (דְּלָתַיִם) and gates (וּשְׁעָרִים) opened before Cyrus, “and gates will not be shut”.
Moses stood “in the gate of the camp” and said, “Who is for Yahweh? To me.”
“The gate of the court” is a screen twenty cubits wide on four pillars.
The gates of the city in Ezekiel's vision are named for the tribes of Israel, three on each side (48:31–34).

senses.gloss: the gate as the place of the elders, judgment and trade
senses.definition: The open place at the gate, where the elders sat, the king or judges heard cases, transactions were made before witnesses, and goods were sold. To do justice “in the gate” is to do it in the city's court.

evidence.note: “Boaz went up to the gate and sat down there”, and called the kinsman to sit with the ten elders.
“All the people who were in the gate (בַּשַּׁעַר) and the elders said, Witnesses!”
The rebellious son is brought “to the elders of his city and to the gate of his place”.
The girl's parents bring the evidence “to the elders of the city, to the gate (הַשָּׁעְרָה)”.
The widow goes up “to the gate, to the elders” when her husband's brother refuses.
Ephron answers Abraham “before all who came in at the gate of his city”, and the field is made sure before them (23:18).
“Hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate (בַשַּׁעַר מִשְׁפָּט).”
“They hate him who reproves in the gate.”
Taking a bribe, “they turn aside the needy in the gate”.
“Judge with truth and the justice of peace in your gates.”
Absalom stands beside the way of the gate to meet every man who has a case for the king.
“The king is sitting in the gate”, and all the people came before him.
“Her husband is known in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land.”
“Elders have ceased from the gate.”
Flour and barley sold for a shekel “in the gate of Samaria”: the market.
They lay a snare for “him who reproves in the gate”.
“Those who sit in the gate (יֹשְׁבֵי שָׁעַר) talk of me.”

senses.definition: In the law, “within your gates” is within the towns where Israel lives, each with its gate, as against the place Yahweh chooses.

evidence.note: “The Levite … and the stranger and the fatherless and the widow who are within your gates (בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ) shall come and eat and be satisfied.”
“Judges and officers you shall appoint in all your gates which Yahweh your God is giving you, by your tribes.”
“If his enemy besieges him in the land of his gates (בְּאֶרֶץ שְׁעָרָיו).”
The sabbath rest is for “your stranger who is within your gates”.
“The Levite who is within your gates”, who has no portion or inheritance.
The law is read to all, with “your stranger who is within your gates”.
“It will besiege you in all your gates, until your high and fortified walls come down.”

senses.gloss: the gate for the city, its people or its power
senses.definition: The gate stands for the city itself, its people, or the strength of an enemy: to possess the gate is to hold the city.

evidence.note: “Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies (וְיִרַשׁ זַרְעֲךָ אֵת שַׁעַר אֹיְבָיו).”
Rebekah's blessing: “may your seed possess the gate of those who hate him (שַׁעַר שֹׂנְאָיו)”.
“All the gate of my people (כָּל־ שַׁעַר עַמִּי) knows that you are a woman of worth”: the townsfolk.
“Wail, gate! Cry out, city!” in parallel.
“Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity.”

senses.gloss: gate of Yahweh's house, of the king's palace
senses.definition: The gates of the courts of Yahweh's house, through which the worshippers came in and which the gatekeepers kept, and the gate of the king's court.

evidence.note: “Stand in the gate of the house of Yahweh … all Judah who enter these gates (בַּשְּׁעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה) to bow down to Yahweh.”
The gatekeepers set at the gates of the house of Yahweh, “so that none who was unclean in anything should enter”.
“Enter his gates with thanksgiving, his courts with praise.”
“The glory of Yahweh came into the house by the way of the gate facing east.”
“This gate shall be shut … for Yahweh, the God of Israel, has entered by it.”
The east gate of the inner court is shut the six working days and opened on the sabbath and the new moon.
The princes of Judah sit “in the entrance of the New Gate of Yahweh” to judge Jeremiah.
Mordecai “sitting in the king's gate (בְּשַׁעַר־ הַמֶּלֶךְ)”, the place of the king's officers.
None might enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.

senses.gloss: gates of death, of the grave; gate of heaven; gates of righteousness
senses.definition: The entrance of a realm or state, spoken of as a city's gate: the gates of death and of the grave, which shut in the dead; the gate of heaven; the gates of righteousness and of Yahweh, by which the righteous enter.

evidence.note: Hezekiah: “in the quiet of my days I will go into the gates of the grave (בְּשַׁעֲרֵי שְׁאוֹל)”.
“Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?”
Yahweh, “who lifts me up from the gates of death (מִשַּׁעֲרֵי מָוֶת)”.

Jacob at Bethel: “this is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (שַׁעַר הַשָּׁמָיִם)”.

“This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous shall enter by it.”
“Lift up your heads, O gates … that the King of glory may come in”; also 24:9.
“Open the gates, that the righteous nation which keeps faithfulness may enter.”

senses.definition: The man at the city gate who opens it and passes word between those outside and the king within.

evidence.note: “The watchman called to the gatekeeper (אֶל־ הַשֹּׁעֵר).”
The lepers “called to the gatekeeper of the city (שֹׁעֵר הָעִיר)”.

“The gatekeepers were on the four sides: east, west, north and south.”

The divisions of the gatekeepers, of the Korahites.
The sons of the gatekeepers who returned from Babylon.

“The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates.”

evidence.note: “To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice.”
The doorkeeper at the high priest's court; also 18:17.

words.summary: Once, Gen 26:12. Its key in the database counts eight more tokens, all שְׁעָרִים “gates” (Jdg 5:8; Isa 26:2; Psa 24:7…), filed with it by spelling. Arabic siʿr “price, rate” shows š and ʿ behind its letters, against ṯ and ġ for the gate: a second older root in the same spelling, so the gate's cognates count against it (balance −3).

senses.definition: A measure as reckoned or estimated; “a hundred measures” is a hundred times the reckoned amount.

evidence.note: “Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundred measures (מֵאָה שְׁעָרִים), and Yahweh blessed him.”

words.summary: Once, Pro 23:7. Its key in the database counts two more tokens, the noun שָׁעַר “gate” in pause (Isa 24:12; Psa 69:13), filed with it by spelling. Like the noun “measure”, it goes with Arabic siʿr (š, ʿ), another older root than the gate's ṯġr, whose cognates therefore count against it (balance −3).

senses.definition: To reckon or calculate inwardly: the grudging host counts the cost of what he offers while he says “eat and drink”.

evidence.note: “For as he reckons in his soul (כְּמּוֹ שָׁעַר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ), so is he. ‘Eat and drink’, he says to you, but his heart is not with you.”

words.summary: Four times, in Jeremiah and Hosea, of Israel's own deeds; Jer 18:13 spells it שַׁעֲרֻרִת and Hos 6:10 שַׁעֲרוּרִיָּה. No cognate has been found that shares its meaning, so the root's cognates (gate, price) count against it: its tie to this root is not understood. It may belong with שׂער “bristle, shudder”, though the text points it with shin.

senses.definition: A deed so foul that it appals: idolatry, adultery and falsehood among Yahweh's own people.

evidence.note: “A desolation and a horror (שַׁמָּה וְשַׁעֲרוּרָה) has come to pass in the land”: the prophets prophesy falsely and the people love it so (5:31).
“In the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: committing adultery and walking in falsehood … they are all to me like Sodom.”
“The virgin of Israel has done a very horrible thing (שַׁעֲרֻרִת)”: forgetting Yahweh for vanity (18:15).
“In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing (שַׁעֲרוּרִיָּה): Ephraim's harlotry is there; Israel is defiled.”

words.summary: Once, Jer 29:17, of figs; Jer 24:2–3 says the same of the bad figs with רָעוֹת “bad”. No cognate shares its meaning, so its tie to the root is not understood.

senses.definition: So bad as not to be eaten: said of figs that stand for the people left in Jerusalem under judgment.

evidence.note: “I will make them like the vile figs (כַּתְּאֵנִים הַשֹּׁעָרִים) that cannot be eaten for badness.”
The same figs: “very bad figs, which cannot be eaten for badness”.

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel. Aramaic writes ת for the older ṯ and keeps ע for ġ, with the last two letters in the other order (t-r-ʿ against ṯ-ġ-r); the same word as Hebrew שַׁעַר.

senses.definition: The king's gate as the place where his officers sat, as in Hebrew שַׁעַר הַמֶּלֶךְ.

evidence.note: Daniel's companions were set over the province, “and Daniel was in the gate of the king (בִּתְרַע מַלְכָּא)”.
The Hebrew phrase: Mordecai sitting in the king's gate.

senses.definition: The door or mouth of a furnace.

evidence.note: “Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the burning fiery furnace (לִתְרַע אַתּוּן נוּרָא).”

senses.gloss: gatekeeper of the house of God
senses.definition: The temple gatekeepers, named among the priests, Levites and singers.

evidence.note: No tribute is to be laid on “the priests and Levites, singers, gatekeepers (תָרָעַיָּא), Nethinim” or servants of the house of God.

senses.gloss: gate (of a city, the temple, the holy city)
senses.definition: The gate of a city or of the temple.

evidence.note: “When he drew near to the gate of the city (לתַרעָא דַּמדִינתָּא), a dead man was being carried out.”
The lame man laid “at the gate of the temple (בּתַרעָא דּהַיכּלָא) called Beautiful”.
The city “has twelve gates (תַּרעֵא), and on the gates twelve angels”, with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel.
“Its gates will not be shut by day.”

senses.gloss: door (of a room, house or tomb)
senses.definition: The door of a room or house, and the opening of a rock-cut tomb.

evidence.note: “Enter your room and shut your door (תַּרעָך).”
A great stone rolled against “the door of the tomb”; also Mrk 16:3.
“The doors were shut where the disciples were.”

senses.definition: “The face of the door”: the veil before the holy of holies.

evidence.note: “The face of the door of the temple (אַפַּי תַּרעָא דּהַיכּלָא) was torn in two from top to bottom.”
A way of life opened “through the veil, which is his flesh”.
The holy of holies is within the second veil.

senses.definition: The way into life or into the kingdom, which Jesus is; the gates of the grave; an opening for the word.

“Enter by the narrow gate”; the gate that leads to life is small (7:14).

God “had opened a door of faith to the nations”.

words.summary: Once in the New Testament. Arabic ṯaġara is to break a wall so as to make a gap; here it is blood breaking out of the body. The link to the gate is the breach or opening. Only Arabic supports it, and Arabic siʿr, of the other older root, counts against it (balance −1): a weak tie, resting on one verse.

senses.definition: Of blood: to break out and flow.

evidence.note: “A woman whose blood had been flowing (דַּתרִיע הוָא דּמָה) twelve years.”

cognates.gloss: gap, breach, opening; frontier pass, the way of access into a country; front teeth; (verb ثَغَرَ) break (a wall) so as to make a gap

evidence.note: “Any gap, opening, interstice, or open intervening space, in a mountain, or in the bottom of a valley, or in a road”; “A frontier-way of access to a country … like a gap in a wall, from which one fears the invasion of the robber”; “This is a city in which are gaps, or breaches.”
“He broke it; namely, a part of a wall … he broke it … so as to make a gap in it”; also “He stopped up … the gap, or breach.”
“gap, cleft, interstice”; “frontier place”; compared with Aramaic תַּרְעָא, Ugaritic ṯġr “gate” and Hebrew שַׁעַר.

cognates.note: The gate is the gap in the wall: the place an enemy would break through, and the city's way in and out. Arabic ṯ and ġ keep apart the sounds that Hebrew writes with ש and ע.

evidence.note: ṯġr KTU 1.119:26 “gate” (H. šaʿar); ṯġr KTU 1.114:11, 1.78:3 “gatekeeper” (H. šōʿēr, cf. Aram. tarāʿ). The scan's OCR drops the diacritics.
Two nouns: “gate” and “gatekeeper”; compared with Hebrew שַׁעַר, Aramaic תַּרְעָא and Arabic ثَغْر.

evidence.note: “The current price, or rate, at which a thing is to be sold.”
“He assigned to it a known and fixed price: or he declared its current price, or the rate at which it should be sold.”
“price”; “Compare Hebrew שער.”

cognates.note: Arabic s answers to Hebrew š, and ʿ to ʿ: another older root than the gate's ṯġr. A price is a reckoned amount, as שַׁעַר “measure” and the verb “reckon”. Arabic سعر also means kindling fire, which has no Hebrew counterpart here.

doctrine.statement: Hezekiah, sick to death, said “I will go into the gates of the grave (שַׁעֲרֵי שְׁאוֹל)”, and when he was healed gave the reason: “the grave does not thank you, death does not praise you … the living, the living, he thanks you, as I do today” (Isa 38:10, 18–19). Job is asked whether the gates of death have been revealed to him (Job 38:17), and the psalmist calls Yahweh the one who lifts him up from the gates of death (Psa 9:14; 107:18). The grave is spoken of as a city whose gates close on the dead, where there is no praise, and only Yahweh brings out. Jesus says of his ecclesia that “the gates of the grave will not prevail against it” (Mat 16:18; Peshitta ותַרעֵא דַּשיֻול, Greek πύλαι ᾅδου, the Septuagint's words in Isa 38:10). From the verses: the dead are shut in the grave, not praising, until God opens it; and the grave will not keep those who are Christ's, who will be brought out by resurrection.

When Abraham had not withheld his only son, Yahweh swore by himself: “I will greatly bless you and greatly multiply your seed … and your seed will possess the gate of his enemies” (Gen 22:16–17); Rebekah's family blessed her with the same words (Gen 24:60). The gate stands for the city and its strength (Rut 3:11; Isa 14:31), so to possess the gate is to hold the enemy's cities. Hebrews takes up this oath (Heb 6:13–14); Zacharias says that the oath sworn to Abraham was that we should be delivered from the hand of our enemies and serve God without fear (Luk 1:71–74); and Paul says the seed is one, “who is Christ” (Gal 3:16). From the verses: the promise is kept in Christ, Abraham's seed, who will hold the gates of his enemies, and in those delivered with him who serve God.

Ezekiel's city has twelve gates, three on each side, “according to the names of the tribes of Israel”, and its name from that day is “Yahweh is there” (Ezk 48:31–35). In Isaiah, Zion's gates stand open continually, not shut day or night, to bring in the wealth of the nations and their kings; her walls are called Salvation and her gates Praise (Isa 60:11, 18). John sees the holy city with twelve gates bearing the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, gates not shut by day, the nations walking in its light and the kings of the earth bringing their glory into it (Rev 21:12–13, 24–26). From the verses: the city of the kingdom bears Israel's tribal names on its gates, and the nations of the earth come into it through gates that stand open.

The psalmist asks, “Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter them”, and answers, “This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous shall enter by it” (Psa 118:19–20), in the psalm whose rejected stone Jesus applies to himself (Psa 118:22; Mat 21:42). Jesus tells his hearers to enter by the narrow gate, for the gate that leads to life is small and few find it (Mat 7:13–14; Luk 13:24), and says, “I am the door: if anyone enters by me he will live” (Jhn 10:9). From the verses: there is one way in to life, the gate of Yahweh, and it is Christ; the righteous enter by it, and those who do not enter are shut out.

note: Root: שער, the database's key (BDB files the gate, the gatekeeper, the measure, the verb “reckon” and the horror words under it); no other entry had it. The sin words (שֵׂעָר hair, שְׂעֹרָה barley, שָׂעִיר) are the entry `sair`, root שׂער. Aramaic and Peshitta words have root תרע (ṯ > ת, with metathesis of the last two letters). Two older roots in one spelling: *ṯġr gate (Arabic ṯaġr, Ugaritic ṯġr) and *šʿr reckon, price (Arabic siʿr). BDB keys: v.fa.aa and v.fc.aa are root headings with no tokens; v.fc.ad (שַׁעֲרִירִיָּה, BDB's שַׁעֲרֻרִית) shares all its tokens (Jer 5:30; 18:13; 23:14) with v.fc.ac, so only v.fc.ac is named and the forms are senses' evidence of one word; Hos 6:10 שַׁעֲרוּרִיָּה has no BDB key in the database. v.fb.ab counts 8 gate tokens and v.fb.aa 2, by spelling (see those words' summaries). Left out: שַׁעֲרַיִם Shaaraim (v.fa.ae), a place; שַׁעַשְׁגַּז Shaashgaz (v.fc.ae), the Persian eunuch of Est 2:14, a Persian name not formed from this root. Name entry: sheariah (v.fa.ad). Peshitta lemmas are copied from the database's vocalised forms (תַּרעָא Mat 7:14; תּרַע SEDRA form; the doorkeeper from וַלתָֿרעָא Mrk 13:34 with prefix and rafe removed); Jhn 10:3 and 18:16–17 have נָטַר תַּרעָא “keeper of the door” and are counted under the gate word. Leads not followed: Segert's glossary also lists /ṯ-ʿ-r/ yṯʿr KTU 1.24:35 “to arrange”(?), just before ṯġr, read only in garbled OCR; if it is ṯʿr it would clash with Arabic s in siʿr, so it is left out until DULAT is checked. Geʿez saʿara “remove, tear” (Anderson–Moser SEM000881 ṯġr[break]V, GEZ004789) not checked in Dillmann or Leslau. Old South Arabian ṯġr not found in Biella's OCR. Jewish Aramaic שַׁעֲרָא “market price, measure” (Jastrow) not cited; check whether Arabic siʿr could be an Aramaic loan, which would weaken it as evidence for a separate root. The horror words: no cognate found; Akkadian šaḫarratu was not found in Oracc; a link with שׂער “bristle, shudder” (entry `sair`, Jer 2:12) is open. Psalms are cited by Hebrew numbering; the macula-lxx locator for Psa 118:20 gives the LXX number too.
